title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
The page finishes Problem 69 from the previous page: determine the residues of the cubes 1, 2^3, 3^3, … modulo a prime P.

Method. Let a be a primitive root mod P. Every x prime to P satisfies x ≡ a^λ, so x^3 ≡ a^{3λ}. The cubic residues are therefore the terms of the geometric progression 1, a^3, a^6, …. That progression returns to 1 at the least λ with (P−1) | 3λ, and that least λ equals the number of distinct cubic residues.

Case I, P = 3n+1. Here λ = n. The cubic residues are 1, a^3, …, a^{3n−3}, since a^{3n} ≡ 1. So exactly n of the P−1 nonzero classes are cubes, and the remaining 2n are cubic non-residues. In modern terms, the cubing map on the cyclic group (Z/P)^* of order 3n is 3-to-1 onto the subgroup of index 3.

Case II, P = 3n+2. Since gcd(3, 3n+1) = 1, the least λ is 3n+1. The progression 1, a^3, …, a^{9n} has 3n+1 = P−1 distinct terms, so every nonzero residue is a cube and there are no non-residues. Cubing is a bijection.

Corollary 1 (§70). For primes P ≡ 1 (mod 3), namely 7, 13, 19, 31, 37, 43, 61, 67, 73, 79, 97, …, there are only n cubic residues and 2n non-residues.

Corollary 2 (§71). Divide 1^3, …, (3n)^3 by P = 3n+1. These 3n cubes give all the cubic residues and there are only n of them, so each residue occurs exactly three times. In other words, there are always three cubes below P^3 with the same residue.

The purpose is Euler's systematic group-theoretic (primitive-root) treatment of power residues in E449. The next page goes on to tables and to the cube roots of unity mod p (1 − f + f^2 ≡ 0, g ≡ −f^2).
errors: No mathematical errors. In case II, λ = 3n+1 is correct because gcd(3, 3n+1) = 1. The final term a^{9n} = a^{3(3n+1)−3} is correct. The list of primes ≡ 1 (mod 3) below 100 is complete and correct.
Minor imprecision: 'omnes plane numeri divisore P minores' means the nonzero numbers below P; residue 0 (from multiples of P) is tacitly set aside.

ideas.what: Counting cubic residues mod p via a primitive root: there are (p−1)/3 cubic residues if p ≡ 1 (mod 3); every nonzero class is a cube if p ≡ 2 (mod 3).
ideas.modern_name: Number of k-th power residues = (p−1)/gcd(k, p−1); index of the subgroup of cubes in a cyclic group
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E262 and later), systematised by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), Section III
ideas.where_published: E262 'Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta' (1761); Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792), chapters on cubic residues; E449 itself

ideas.what: The cubing map is 3-to-1 on (Z/p)^* for p ≡ 1 (mod 3): every cubic residue arises from exactly three cubes among 1^3, …, (p−1)^3.
ideas.modern_name: Kernel of the cubing homomorphism (the cube roots of unity mod p) has order 3

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, correct exposition of cubic-residue counting via primitive roots. The material is well known and already credited to Euler and Gauss.
transcription_corrections: Case II progression: the image clearly reads '1, a^3, a^6, a^9 …… a^{9n}'. The '[?]' can be removed; a^{9n} is correct.
